lines: One real, foundational paper on this exact subject states this rule directly, in its own words.
Only entries from the leader's own current term are ever committed by counting replicas.
A real, widely used consensus implementation in Rust keeps its own log genuinely separate from the application's own state machine.
That separation is exactly what lets consensus itself be tested against a trivial state machine first.

lines: So here's the real shape of this whole topic: committing is never about a count alone, and repairing is never about guessing where two logs went wrong.
A log entry only counts once a real majority holds it under the exact term the leader is currently running, which is why an old, already-widespread entry still has to wait.
And fixing a broken follower never means special-casing anything; the leader just keeps stepping backward until the numbers finally agree, then lets ordinary replication take it from there.
